import numpy as np, pandas as pd

pk,_=find_peaks(y,prominence=40,width=2)
w=peak_widths(y,pk,rel_height=0.5)[0]*np.mean(np.diff(x))

content.text: The overview is clear. There are two strong real peaks near 127 and 306 cm⁻¹, a single-channel cosmic spike at 327 cm⁻¹, a weak bump near 204 cm⁻¹, and a smooth rising background with noise above 400 cm⁻¹. Next I'll fit the peaks with lmfit on a local baseline to get positions, widths and areas.

input.command:
cd "C:\WINDOWS\TEMP\ramanlens-eval\dev-haiku\bare\syn-GaSe-01" && python -I -c "
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from lmfit import Model
from lmfit.models import VoigtModel, LinearModel, LorentzianModel
d=pd.read_csv('spectrum.csv')
x=d.shift_cm1.values; y=d.intensity.values.copy()
# remove cosmic spike at 327.06 by excluding that single channel
def fit(lo,hi,centre,exclude=None,extra=None,label=''):
    m=(x>=lo)&(x<=hi)
    if exclude is not None: m&=~np.isin(np.round(x,2),exclude)
    xx=x[m]; yy=y[m]
    mod=VoigtModel(prefix='p1_')+LinearModel(prefix='b_')
    p=mod.make_params()
    p['p1_center'].set(value=centre,min=centre-10,max=centre+10)
    p['p1_amplitude'].set(value=yy.max()*0.5,min=0)
    p['p1_sigma'].set(value=2,min=0.1,max=20)
    p['p1_gamma'].set(value=2,min=0.1,max=20)
    p['b_slope'].set(value=0); p['b_intercept'].set(value=np.median(yy[:5]))
    r=mod.fit(yy,p,x=xx)
    c=r.params['p1_center'].value; ce=r.params['p1_center'].stderr
    fw=r.params['p1_fwhm'].value if 'p1_fwhm' in r.params else np.nan
    print(label,'centre %.2f +- %s'%(c,ce),'fwhm(Voigt approx) %.2f'%fw,'chi2red %.1f'%r.redchi,'area %.0f'%(r.params['p1_amplitude'].value))
    return r
r1=fit(105,155,127.5,label='peak127')
r2=fit(285,325,306,exclude=[327.06],label='peak306')
# Lorentzian alt
for lo,hi,c,ex,l in [(105,155,127.5,None,'L127'),(285,325,306,[327.06],'L306')]:
    m=(x>=lo)&(x<=hi)
    if ex: m&=~np.isin(np.round(x,2),ex)
    xx=x[m]; yy=y[m]
    mod=LorentzianModel(prefix='p1_')+LinearModel(prefix='b_')
    p=mod.make_params(p1_center=c,p1_amplitude=yy.max()*np.pi*2,p1_sigma=2,b_slope=0,b_intercept=np.median(yy[:5]))
    r=mod.fit(yy,p,x=xx)
    print(l,'centre %.2f +- %s fwhm %.2f redchi %.1f'%(r.params['p1_center'].value,r.params['p1_center'].stderr,2*r.params['p1_sigma'].value,r.redchi))
"

mod1=LorentzianModel(prefix='a_')+LinearModel(prefix='bg_')

print('noise std of baseline 160-260 region (detrended):', np.std(np.diff(y[(x>160)&(x<260)]))/np.sqrt(2))
"

input.command:
cd "C:\WINDOWS\TEMP\ramanlens-eval\dev-haiku\bare\syn-GaSe-01" && python -I -c "
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from scipy.sparse import diags, identity
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve
d=pd.read_csv('spectrum.csv')
x=d.shift_cm1.values; y=d.intensity.values.copy()
# remove single-channel cosmic ray by interpolation
i=np.argmin(np.abs(x-327.06)); y[i]=0.5*(y[i-1]+y[i+1])
# asymmetric least squares baseline
def als(y,lam=1e5,p=0.01,n=10):
    L=len(y); D=diags([1,-2,1],[0,-1,-2],shape=(L,L-2))
    w=np.ones(L)
    for _ in range(n):
        W=diags(w); Z=W+lam*D.dot(D.T)
        z=spsolve(Z.tocsc(),w*y); w=p*(y>z)+(1-p)*(y<z)
    return z
b=als(y)
r=y-b
# noise: robust std of residual
sig=1.4826*np.median(np.abs(r-np.median(r)))
print('robust noise sigma (counts):',round(sig,1))
pk,pr=find_peaks(r,height=4*sig,width=2)
for p,h,wl in zip(pk,pr['peak_heights'],pr['widths']):
    print(round(x[p],2),'height %.0f  SNR %.1f  width_ch %.1f'%(h,h/sig,wl))
"

candidates.evidence: Three real features: 127.8 cm-1 (strongest), 305.9 cm-1 (second), and a weak broad band at 204.9 cm-1. The 305.9 band is within ~2 cm-1 of the ~308 cm-1 GaSe mode. The 127.8 and 204.9 bands are ~7-8 cm-1 below the ~134.5 and ~213 cm-1 GaSe modes (literature values from memory, not verified in this session), and the intensity pattern is inverted relative to what GaSe usually shows (its ~213 mode is normally among the strongest). Ranked first only because it is the closest layered Ga-chalcogenide match for three peaks in the right region.

Sibling Ga-chalcogenide with a similar mode pattern in the ~130, ~210 and ~305 cm-1 region, so it cannot be ruled out from three peaks. I did not check GaS reference positions in this session, so this is a placeholder for the family, not a verified match.

Its ~205 cm-1 (Eg) and ~314 cm-1 (A1g) modes loosely resemble the weak 204.9 and 305.9 cm-1 bands, but it has no expected band near 128 cm-1 and the 306 band is 8 cm-1 low. Included only as a low-probability alternative; literature values are from memory.

structured_output.hint_reasoning: No material hint was given (material_hint null), so this is an identify task. The spectrum shows three real Raman features, not a clean match for GaSe. The 305.9 band agrees with GaSe's ~308 cm-1 mode, but the 127.8 and 204.9 bands sit ~7-8 cm-1 below the expected ~134.5 and ~213 cm-1 modes, which is more than typical calibration error at 295 K. The intensity pattern is also inverted relative to GaSe. The best supported answer is a GaSe-family layered Ga-chalcogenide with moderate-to-low confidence. Literature positions are from memory and not verified in this session (no database or internet access), so the call rests mainly on the peak pattern.

limits: The material is not uniquely identified. Only three features are significant, two of them sit ~7-8 cm-1 from the GaSe modes, and the intensity pattern does not match GaSe. Confidence in GaSe is moderate-to-low.
No polarization or angle series was measured (single spectrum, backscattering along the layer normal), so no symmetry labels (irreps or polarization patterns) can be assigned from this data.
Literature reference positions are from memory and were not checked against a database; the GaS and SnS2 comparisons are based on approximate recall, not verified values.
The spectrum covers only 60-1100 cm-1, so low-frequency shear and breathing modes (typically below 60 cm-1 in layered chalcogenides) and any higher-frequency modes cannot be checked.

No Si 520.7 cm-1 reference line is present, so there is no internal calibration. The ~7-8 cm-1 offsets cannot be separated from calibration error or a different material, and a 295 K temperature effect is unlikely to account for them.
The broad continuum rising above 400 cm-1 is luminescence-like or noise, not a Raman band; no features above ~350 cm-1 pass the significance test.
The single-channel spike at 327.06 cm-1 (~10900 counts on a ~2000 background) is a cosmic ray and was removed before fitting. The 288 cm-1 point is the left wing of the 306 band, not a separate peak.
